specialFocus.title: Read the Bottle — Hydro Dates, the Star, and What's Expired
specialFocus.why:
Every breathing-air bottle we carry has a hydro date: SCBA bottles, 5-minute escape packs, and cascade and work-unit bottles. It's the month and year the bottle was last pressure-tested (a hydrostatic test) by a DOT-licensed retester. That test is the only proof the bottle will still hold thousands of psi without letting go. Once the hydro runs out, nobody has proven the bottle is safe, so it doesn't go to work. Customers and auditors check this first, and it takes ten seconds to read. Alex, if you can, bring a steel, an aluminum, and a composite bottle to pass around.

1 · Where to look and how to read it (steel & aluminum: stamped on the shoulder)
2 · Which bottle is it? Each type runs its own clock
STEEL · DOT-3A / 3AA
Heavy, painted, dates stamped in the metal. Most cascade bottles.
Hydro every 5 years.
With a ★ right after the newest date: every 10 years.
ALUMINUM · DOT-3AL
Lighter, bare or painted metal, dates stamped on the shoulder.
Hydro every 5 years.
No star rule for aluminum. A star here buys nothing.
COMPOSITE · carbon wrap
Light, fiber-wrapped. Label reads DOT-SP, DOT-E or DOT-CFFC. Most SCBA & escape bottles.
Hydro every 5 years (some older fiberglass: 3, so check the label).
PLUS a life limit: 15 years from the date it was made (30 only if the label says 30-year). Dates are on labels, never stamped.
★ THE STAR: what it gives you, and when it doesn't count
  • What it means: the steel bottle passed its test under DOT's 10-year rule, so the next hydro is due in 10 years instead of 5.
  • Steel only (DOT-3A / 3AA). A star on aluminum or composite gives you nothing.
  • It has to sit right after the newest date. A star next to an older test doesn't carry forward. If the latest date has no star, it's a 5-year bottle.
  • Struck-out or X'd-out star = back to 5 years. That happens when the bottle was filled with a gas that isn't on DOT's list. The star is only for clean, dry gases like breathing air and nitrogen, and never for underwater (scuba) breathing.
  • A PLUS sign (+) is not a star. It means the steel bottle may be filled 10% over its stamped pressure. It adds zero time to the hydro date.
3 · Composite bottles run two clocks, and either one can kill it
Why we're stricter than the bare DOT minimum: DOT lets a bottle that was filled before its due date stay in service until it's empty. Canon doesn't run on that. Nobody can look at a bottle and know when it was filled, and the customer's auditor only sees the date. Past its month = off the trailer.
Sources: DOT 49 CFR 180.205 (requalification), 180.209 (retest intervals and the 10-year star rule), 180.213 (marking format, composite labels); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.134 (i)(4) and (h)(3)(iii); the composite bottle's own DOT special permit. Drawings are examples, not real serial numbers.
specialFocus.standardLabel: The Bottle Standard: Check It Before It Goes to Work
standard: Read the newest date on every bottle before it goes on a trailer or into service: month, retester ID in the square, year. Do the math out loud: +5 years, or +10 only if it's a steel bottle with a star right after that newest date.

A bottle is good through the last day of its due month. On the 1st of the next month it's expired: tag it OUT OF HYDRO, pull it off the trailer, and tell your lead so the shop can send it out. Due this month? Flag it now, not on the 31st.

The star is steel only. No star, a star next to an older date, or a struck-out star means 5 years. Aluminum and composite bottles never get 10 years from a star. A plus sign (+) is about fill pressure and adds no time.

Composite = two clocks. Check the hydro label (every 5 years) AND the manufacture date (15-year life, 30 only if the label says 30-year). If either one is up, the bottle is done. Never stamp, scratch, or write on a composite wrap or its labels.
Damage beats the date. Dents, gouges, bulges, heat or fire marks, chemical stains, cut or fuzzy fibers on a composite, or a label you can't read: out of service no matter how fresh the hydro is.

In date AND full. SCBA and escape bottles stay fully charged and get refilled before they drop below 90% (OSHA 1910.134). Found one out of hydro, damaged, or low? Put it on your readiness form with the bottle number and who you told.

scenarios.title: The Cascade Walk-Around
scenarios.body: You're setting the air trailer on location and read three steel 3AA cascade bottles. Bottle A: 09 [A123] 16 ★. Bottle B: 03 [A123] 22, no star. Bottle C: 11 [A123] 21, no star. Today is November 2026. Which ones are good, which one is expired, and which one needs a call to the shop this week? (A: due Sept 2026, so EXPIRED; pull it. B: good through March 31, 2027. C: due this month, good through Nov 30; flag it today.)

scenarios.title: The Escape Pack With a Fresh Hydro
scenarios.body: A 5-minute escape pack has a composite bottle with a shiny hydro label from 2023. Someone says, 'It just got tested, it's fine.' You flip it over: the label says it was made in October 2011 with a 15-year service life. Is it fine? (No. The life clock ran out in October 2026. A fresh hydro doesn't bring a composite bottle back from its life limit. Tag it, pull it, tell your lead.)

questions: Pick up your SCBA or escape bottle. Where's the newest hydro date? Read it out loud and tell us the month it's due.
What does the star give you, and which bottles can never use it?
Star or plus sign: what's the difference, and which one adds time?
Your bottle's due month is this month. Is it good tomorrow? Is it good on the 1st?
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: If you can't read the date, can't do the math, or it's past its month, the bottle does not go to work. Tag it, pull it, and tell your lead. A bottle out of hydro is a bottle nobody has proven will hold.

before.title: Working Around Mobile Equipment — Alex's Good and Bad From the Field
before.why:
Alex, this one's yours. It comes from Matt's nightly form reviews (10/28 to 11/4) and the crew's own OWL write-ups on this week's topic (10/21 to 10/29). First, the good news: those reviews show no mobile-equipment incident or near miss. The crews are doing the hard part well around cranes, forklifts and trucks. Where we're slipping is the part before the job: the trailer, the gear and telling someone.

✓ THE GOOD: say these names
  • Dawson Drake & Dermont Morgan, Brook D-W23I (10/21): the forklift spotter kept a safe distance and kept talking to the driver.
  • Pablo Soto & Baldemar Bracomontes, Jack Mohr (10/22): made the exclusion zones known to the crane crew and the truckers, so nobody had to guess.
  • Raymundo Solis & Kedrick McCarter, Hernandez 20 #1 (10/22): used a hold point before the crane, kept everyone clear of the suspended load, and stood away from the pump truck's pressure hose.
  • Michael Jobe, Brook D 17H (10/29): the vac truck wasn't sucking. Jobe spoke up and the crew stood by for another truck instead of working around it.
  • Bryan Medlin, trailer 604 (11/2): found broken welds on the cascade rack, put it on both forms, and named who was told. That's how it's done.
  • Ralph Forbes, Crouch 16 (11/4): when the vac truck didn't show, the crew changed the plan and wrote down exactly what happened. Fullest write-up of the day.
  • Bobby Galindo, Nail Tillman (11/2): heard a hiss during a flow-line reconnect, stopped the crew and moved them back until it was fixed and tested. That's stop work used for real, so tick utilized, not discussed.
  • Trailer GPS (10/30 report): 3 trailers flagged and the longest outage is 5 days. On 9/28 it was 123.
✗ THE BAD: fix these this week
  • Trailers rolling with known defects. Trailer 139's doors were flying open on lease roads (11/4). The same trailer's rear door was written up hanging on one bracket on 10/28. A marker light out was written up on 605 two days running (10/29, 10/30), only in a photo note, and the trailer still went out. The standard is no trailer moves unless every light works. Also written up: 604's rack welds (11/2).
  • Zone gear missing. 127 had no cones, caution tape or spotter flags (10/29), and the photos on that form were from 2020. 152 had no cones (10/30). 148 has been short caution tape since 10/29.
  • Problem written, nobody told. Three readiness forms on 11/3 named a problem and no person: a work pack short a mask, caution tape, and mask bags. On 11/4, neither form on 139's doors named anyone either.
  • Old photos. Spotter flags, cones and the cascade alarm are the repeat offenders. One hitch-ball photo was a year old (11/2). An old photo proves nothing about today's hookup.
  • Rain and mud. One rig check says the checklist couldn't be done in the rain but still carries numbers. If you couldn't check it, say so and go back. Crews also reported people slipping on muddy pads.
  • Forms and hydro. At the 11 PM check, 7 air-job trailers were short a required form on 11/3 and 6 on 11/4, and 5 of them each day were SM. That's the same readiness gap from Matt's weekly. Trailer 503's hydro dates were blank again on 11/4, three days running.
On the office, not the crew: the shop ran out of mask bags and stickers, and three techs reported it 11/3. We owe you that resupply.
before.standardLabel: Alex's Five Asks on WAME: Starting This Morning
standard: Talk to the operator first. Eye contact or radio before you enter any swing or travel zone. If you can't see the mirrors, they can't see you. Ground work stops when equipment moves nearby.
Set the zone with real gear. Cones, caution tape and spotter flags are checked at the trailer inspection. Missing one? Get it before you leave the shop, or write it down and name who you told.

All lights or no move. Check hitch, ball, pins, chains, lights, doors and rack fresh at every hookup. A defect goes in Comments for Management, not a photo note, with who you told. The trailer doesn't roll until a lead clears it.

Every lift gets a spotter and a tag line, and they're two different people. If the crew doesn't have them, that's a hold point. Say so before the load moves, like the crew at Scarlet Unit 2 did on 10/25.

Rain and mud change the plan. Walk the zone again, because trucks stop longer and spotters slip. If weather kept you from checking something, write that and go back when it clears. Today's photo or no photo, never an old one.

scenarios.title: 5 AM at the Shop
scenarios.body: Your inspection finds an amber marker light out. The job's an hour away and the company man is already calling. What do you write, where do you write it, who do you tell, and does the trailer move? Now change it to a door hanging on one bracket, or a broken weld on the cascade rack. (Comments for Management, with the name of who you told. No lights, no move. Get a lead's call before a door or weld defect goes down the road. A late start is cheaper than what can happen on the highway.)

scenarios.title: Mud and a Backing Truck
scenarios.body: The pad is soaked from two days of rain. A vac truck is backing toward the tank, and the spotter slips and drops out of the driver's mirror. Your crew is 30 feet away finishing a connection. What should happen in the next five seconds, who calls it, and how does the driver know? (Anyone can call the stop. The driver stops the moment the spotter disappears from the mirror. Ground work stops until everyone's accounted for. Then re-walk the backing path before it starts again.)

questions: Your last location: who was running the equipment, and how were you talking to them? Radio, hand signals, or just hoping?
When did you last put your hands on your trailer's spotter flags and cones, not a photo of them?

A kill truck operator was wearing an H2S monitor up on a hard hat, above the breathing zone (10/27). Our tech spoke up about where it belongs. What does professional sound like when it's another company's operator?
Alex's question: what did you see around equipment in the last two weeks that nobody wrote down?
before.nonNegotiable: If you can't name who has eyes on you, you're not clear to be there. No spotter, no tag line, no zone gear: stop and get them. And no Canon trailer moves unless every light works.
